paragraphs: The old, weathered manor, Blackwood House, stood in stoic silence against the biting autumn wind. Inside, however, the silence was shattered not by the storm, but by the piercing shriek of Mrs. Gable, the housekeeper. In the grand drawing-room, amidst overturned antique furniture and a scattering of rare coins, lay the lifeless form of Lord Ashworth, his monocle still clutched in a rigid hand, his usually impeccable tweed jacket now stained crimson.

Detective Miles Corbin arrived an hour later, his trench coat pulled tight against the incessant drizzle. He surveyed the scene with a professional calm, his gaze sweeping over the opulent room. Mrs. Gable, a small, tremulous woman, was being comforted by a strapping young man, a chauffeur named Silas, who rarely left Lord Ashworth’s side. Miles noted the raw fear in Mrs. Gable’s eyes, and the quiet, almost watchful intensity in Silas's.

"Tell me what happened, Mrs. Gable," Miles' voice was gentle, but firm. She wrung her hands. "I… I was bringing Lord Ashworth his evening tea, sir. He had been in here for hours, polishing his coin collection. When I opened the door… it was like this. All… all chaos. And him… oh, dear Lord." Her voice trailed off into a sob. Miles nodded, his eyes scanning the various coins scattered across the Persian rug.

Silas stepped forward, his face a mask of concern. "I heard a commotion, sir, a sort of thud, just before Mrs. Gable screamed. I was in the kitchen, checking on the boiler. I ran straight here, but it was too late. He was already… gone." Miles observed Silas's hands; they were large, calloused, but seemed to tremble ever so slightly. He then noticed a small, peculiar silver coin clutched in Lord Ashworth's dead hand, separate from the others.

A third character emerged from the shadow of the hallway, a woman in a flowing silk dress, her face pale but composed. This was Lady Beatrice Ashworth, Lord Ashworth’s estranged niece, who had only recently arrived at Blackwood House after a long absence. Her eyes, though dry, held a deep sorrow. "My uncle… he was such a stickler for order," she murmured, her voice barely a whisper. "To see his collection in such disarray…" She trailed off, gesturing vaguely at the scene.

Miles noticed something odd about Lady Beatrice. Her silk dress, though elegant, had a small, almost imperceptible tear near the hem, and a faint smudge of dark grease on one sleeve. He made a mental note. "Lady Beatrice, when did you last see your uncle?" he inquired. She hesitated, looking towards the large grandfather clock in the corner. "Around six, I believe. He was in here, as usual, absorbed in his coins. I then went to my room to read."

"And you, Silas?" Miles turned to the chauffeur. "Where were you around six?" Silas's brow furrowed. "I was in the garage, sir, performing routine maintenance on the Rolls. Lord Ashworth was quite particular about its upkeep." Miles eyed Silas's powerful build again, then glanced at the scattered coins. The small silver one remained a curiosity, its glint distinct from the duller gold pieces.

Miles knelt beside Lord Ashworth, carefully examining the immediate vicinity. He noticed a faint, almost invisible scratch on the polished mahogany floor near the body, as if something heavy had been dragged. His fingers brushed against a small, metallic shard caught in the rug's fibres, no bigger than a fingernail clipping. It seemed to be from some sort of broken mechanism. He pocketed it, his gaze again drawn to the unique silver coin clutched by the deceased.

A fourth individual, Dr. Alistair Finch, Lord Ashworth's personal physician and a distant cousin, arrived shortly after, having been summoned by Mrs. Gable. He was a portly man with a perpetually anxious expression. His medical bag clutched tightly, he looked at the scene with a mixture of shock and professional detachment. "Oh, my dear Ashworth," he muttered, shaking his head. "To think it would come to this." He offered a brief, perfunctory examination before confirming the obvious.

Miles observed Dr. Finch's hands – soft, manicured, quite unlike Silas's. "Dr. Finch, when did you last see Lord Ashworth?" The doctor sighed, adjusting his spectacles. "I had a standing appointment this morning, as I do every Tuesday. He was in robust health then, for a man his age. He did, however, mention some rather heated words with his chauffeur, Silas, earlier in the week regarding a missing rare coin."

Silas's head snapped up, his eyes flashing. "That's a lie! Lord Ashworth simply asked if I'd seen a particular coin. He was always misplacing things." Miles watched the exchange, noting the anger in Silas’s voice, the quick defensiveness. The doctor simply shrugged, looking uncomfortable. "Just repeating what I heard, my boy. Ashworth was rather particular about his collection, you know." The implication hung heavy in the air.

Miles walked over to the overturned display cabinet where the coins were usually kept. It was a sturdy, heavy piece of furniture, designed to protect valuables. He ran his hand along the broken lock mechanism. It hadn't been picked; it had been forced open with considerable strength. He remembered the scratch on the floor and the metallic shard. Could Silas, with his powerful build, have done this? The question lingered.

Later, as the local constable began processing the scene, Miles spoke privately with Mrs. Gable. "Mrs. Gable, did Lord Ashworth have any enemies?" The housekeeper wrung her apron. "Oh, no, sir! Lord Ashworth was a kind man, if a bit eccentric. But… he did have a fierce temper when provoked. And he was very protective of his coins. He even had a special alarm system installed, though it seems to have failed tonight."

"An alarm system?" Miles raised an eyebrow, looking around the room. There was no visible panel or sensor. "Where was it located?" Mrs. Gable pointed to a small, almost invisible button discreetly placed beneath the edge of the display cabinet. "He pressed it whenever he was handling his most valuable pieces. It would alert him if anyone attempted to open the cabinet without his unique key." Miles pressed it. Nothing happened. The metallic shard he found might be a piece of it.

Lady Beatrice approached Miles, her expression still somber. "Detective, I overheard the discussion about the missing coin. My uncle was indeed very upset about it, even more than usual. He suspected it had been stolen, not merely misplaced. He confided in me that he believed someone close to him was taking advantage of his trust." She glanced pointedly towards Silas, who was now helping a uniformed officer bag evidence.

Silas, catching Lady Beatrice’s glance, stopped what he was doing and glared. "I never stole anything from Lord Ashworth! I cared for him!" His voice was loud, echoing slightly in the large room. Miles intervened smoothly. "Thank you, Lady Beatrice. And Silas, please continue with the officer." The tension in the room was palpable. It seemed everyone had a reason to point a finger at the chauffeur.

Miles returned to the body. He gently pried the silver coin from Lord Ashworth's grasp. It was indeed unusual, with an intricate, almost clockwork-like design on one side. It felt heavier than it looked. He then noticed something else: a small, almost microscopic, dark stain on Lord Ashworth's thumb, directly beneath where he'd clutched the coin. It looked like ink, or perhaps a faint dye.

He considered the scratch on the floor again, the broken alarm, the forced cabinet lock. Silas's strength and his supposed argument with Ashworth over a coin made him a prime suspect. The oil smudge on Beatrice's dress seemed minor in comparison, perhaps from leaning against something. Dr. Finch’s claim about Silas stealing a coin also added to the growing pile of evidence against the chauffeur. Miles knew the evidence was piling up.

Miles then examined the unique silver coin more closely. He saw a tiny, almost invisible seam along its edge, suggesting it wasn't a solid coin at all, but rather two halves fitted together. With a delicate twist, it separated, revealing a miniature, intricately folded piece of paper tucked inside. His breath hitched. This was a message, not a coin.

Unfolding the tiny paper, Miles read the hastily scrawled words. "Silas is innocent. I discovered Finch's deceit. He swapped the real coins for fakes, then poisoned me to silence me. The proof is in the old ledger, under 'Estate Expenditures'… He will come for this coin." The ink on the note was the same as the faint stain on Lord Ashworth's thumb. His dying act was to expose the truth.

Miles looked up, his eyes immediately finding Dr. Finch, who stood by the fireplace, seemingly oblivious, chatting nervously with Mrs. Gable. The doctor had been among the first to examine the body, and it would have been easy for him to suggest the "missing coin" story to divert suspicion, knowing Silas was already on thin ice with Lord Ashworth. The "poisoned me" part was chilling.

The small metallic shard Miles had found earlier resurfaced in his mind. It wasn't from the alarm system. It was too finely crafted. He remembered Dr. Finch's medical bag, specifically the small, delicate instruments he'd seen inside. The scratch on the floor wasn't from dragging the cabinet; it was a lighter, more precise mark, perhaps from a struggle or from something falling.

He approached Dr. Finch, the tiny, folded note still clutched in his hand. "Dr. Finch," Miles began, his voice devoid of emotion, "Lord Ashworth often spoke highly of your discretion. Tell me, how exactly did you manage to replace his most valuable numismatic treasures with convincing forgeries without anyone noticing?" Dr. Finch's face went white. He stammered, "I... I don't know what you mean, Detective."

"Lord Ashworth discovered your scheme," Miles continued, holding up the tiny message. "He was trying to expose you. He even noted the poisoning and where to find the evidence of your theft – the old ledger under 'Estate Expenditures'." Dr. Finch's eyes darted frantically towards the grand library. His hands trembled, not from anxiety, but from a sudden, stark fear. He lunged for the 'coin' in Miles's hand, confirming his guilt.

Uniformed officers quickly subdued Dr. Finch. The medical examiner later confirmed a rapid-acting, undetectable poison in Lord Ashworth's system, confirming the note's claim. Miles found the ledger exactly where the note indicated, detailing suspicious "medical supply" expenditures that perfectly matched the value of the missing rare coins. The scratch on the floor was from Dr. Finch struggling to extract the 'coin' from Lord Ashworth's dying grasp after the poison had been administered, a struggle that had also broken the tiny alarm and overturned the cabinet. Silas, the distracting character, was cleared, his anger now understood as grief. Justice, finally, had been served at Blackwood House.
